title: DNA Methylation-Based Biological Age Prediction in Colon Tissue
goal: Predict the biological age of normal and healthy colon samples in the DNA methylation data from the genomicsclass GitHub page, using PCA to identify age-associated principal components, CpG feature selection, regression modelling, and comparison of predicted biological age between normal and cancer tissues.
context: I chose a DNA methylation-based age prediction problem using a public colon DNA methylation dataset. The workflow uses high-dimensional epigenomic data and involves PCA, identification of age-associated principal components, CpG feature selection, regression modelling, model diagnostics, prediction, and statistical comparison between normal and cancer tissues. This is more complex than Session 1 because it involves several interconnected statistical decisions and requires dimensionality reduction and feature selection before modelling. Using AI throughout the workflow does not substantially change my choice of problem because I already use AI as an assistant for code development, troubleshooting, statistical reasoning, and interpretation, while I retain responsibility for evaluating and making the final analytical decisions.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: I completed the planned workflow and obtained outputs for all major analytical steps. Claude was useful for reviewing code, explaining statistical procedures, and helping move between steps. However, even though Claude highlighted particular statistical limitations, it did not consistently highlight the fact that >I had a small sample size, which could lead to instability. It only judged based on ideal conditions. I would hope that it adapts to contexts where datasets are few and tailors suggestions that will consider this.

Step 5.step_name: Build and evaluate the DNA methylation-based age prediction model.
Step 5.step_action: Fit a multiple linear regression model using the selected CpG methylation features to predict chronological age. Evaluate the fitted model using model-summary statistics and diagnostic analyses, then generate a predicted methylation-derived age for each sample and compare predicted with chronological age.

nodes.label: Fit the regression model on the 24 selected CpGs
nodes.detail: The participant initially fits an initial linear model, finding it badly overfit; he flags this as 'Claude misled me'. Given the small sample size, he decides to skip FDR/Bonferroni-based multi-PC selection and instead stick to PC2 (the single most significantly age-correlated component, p=0.02), extracting its rotation/loading vector and selecting the top 24 CpGs by absolute loading magnitude. The participant fits lm(age ~ ., data) using the properly-selected 24 age-related CpGs and reviews summary(lmod): with 26 samples and 24 predictors the model is still nearly saturated (F-test p~0.48, 1 residual df), but this is a substantial improvement over the earlier degenerate all-NA model.

user_response.label: modify
user_response.reasoning: The user takes the initially adopted code from r15, realizes that Claude didn't give him what he asked for, and changes it here.

nodes.label: Run model diagnostics on the fitted regression
nodes.detail: The participant runs diagnostic plots (Q-Q residuals) and a Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals (W=0.954, p=0.29), finding no departure from normality.

nodes.detail: Claude confirms no clear assumption violations but attributes this partly to the model being heavily overfit given the very small sample (26 observations, 24 predictors).

nodes.label: Review the response about reviewing diagnostics (no violations) and note the model is heavily overfit.

nodes.detail: The participant predicts each sample's methylation-derived 'biological' age with predict(lmod, t_meth) and computes the correlation between predicted and actual chronological age, obtaining a very strong correlation (r = 0.991).

nodes.detail: Claude explains the strong in-sample correlation is expected given the overfit model (predictors fit to 26 samples means the model has essentially memorized the training data), that it does not validate the CpGs as real age predictors, and recommends leave-one-out cross-validation or regularization for an honest performance estimate.

nodes.detail: The participant runs Welch two-sample t-tests comparing (a) predicted ages and (b) actual chronological ages between the normal and cancer groups; both come back non-significant, showing no statistically detectable age difference between the groups.
